title: Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
content:
This thread discusses a project by the user `fireflyk64`, who spent a decade reverse-engineering the classic DOS game *Wing Commander* to add multiplayer functionality. By manually mapping the game's memory—including identifying the camera's entity slot—the author successfully synced game states to allow for cooperative play. The author later utilized AI to assist in porting the networking stack to WebRTC for browser-based play and to compile the project.

**Key highlights from the discussion:**

*   **Project Accessibility:** Users can play the modded game in a browser via DOSBox. Since game files aren't hosted, users can drag in their own installer, or play a provided open-source "DOS Vega Strike" version if they lack the original files.
*   **The "Hacking" Journey:** Many commenters shared nostalgic stories of "memory hacking" in the 8-bit/DOS era—manually identifying memory offsets for values like money or health. This was compared to modern techniques using tools like Cheat Engine or automated freezer cartridges (on systems like the C64).
*   **AI in Development:** The author acknowledged using AI to modernize the codebase and port the game for web browser compatibility. While some users were impressed by the integration, the author emphasized that the core, difficult reverse-engineering work was done entirely by hand over the last eight years.
*   **Community Interaction:** The thread saw a reunion between the author and long-time community members from the *Vega Strike* era, highlighting the longevity of the space-sim modding community.
*   **Technical Discussions:** There is a brief sidebar regarding networking protocols, specifically the author's decision to keep voice data on a separate WebRTC stream to ensure game data packets maintain priority. Additionally, another developer shared their own native ARM64/WASM decompilation project for the game, leading to a constructive exchange on using modern WebRTC-based lobby systems.

title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
content:
The developers of Linum AI shared their new text-to-image model, **Pyramid-JiT**, which they trained for ~$20K. The core innovation is a pixel-space diffusion architecture that bypasses the traditional Variational Autoencoder (VAE), resulting in faster convergence and more efficient inference. They released the model weights under an Apache 2.0 license as a stepping stone toward their ultimate goal of building high-control, affordable generative video tools.

**Key discussion points from the community:**

*   **Efficiency vs. Capability:** Users were impressed by the $20K training cost for an image model. While some debated whether big labs are disincentivized from pursuing efficiency (due to profit models favoring compute-intensive "intelligence"), others noted that internal efficiency is likely a hidden priority for maintaining profit margins.
*   **Technical Curiosity:** Commenters expressed surprise that removing the VAE yielded high-quality results. There was significant interest in the "recipe" behind the training, with users asking for more transparency regarding the 660M-image dataset, data sourcing (avoiding "piracy"), and how to replicate the process for smaller, specialized experiments.
*   **Model Performance:** Observations of the output noted typical diffusion model artifacts, such as mangled hands/limbs and "uncanny" textures. Some users questioned how much the showcase results were cherry-picked, while others were optimistic about potential future optimizations, such as quantization for browser-based WebGPU execution.
*   **Future Directions:** The discussion touched on the importance of iterative creative control for animation. The authors and community discussed research directions for video generation, including efficient attention implementations and "reflow" techniques to reduce iteration steps.

The model is available on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/Linum-AI/pjit-21k), and the research background is documented on the [Linum AI website](https://www.linum.ai/field-notes/pjit-21k).

title: Show HN: I built a tool that prices a pre-built PC part by part
content:
The thread discusses the launch of **PCDealCheck**, a tool designed to evaluate the value of pre-built PCs by parsing listings, identifying components, and comparing them against a daily-updated pricing engine.

### Key takeaways:
*   **Core Value Proposition:** Users can paste a link to a pre-built PC to receive a "value grade" and a component-by-component cost breakdown. The developer distinguishes this from PCPartPicker by noting that it is an automated, "reverse" lookup designed for quick decision-making rather than manual building.
*   **Current Limitations:** The tool is currently a self-financed prototype limited to the U.S. market due to API costs and usage quotas. Several users expressed interest in support for other regions (Canada, Australia, Europe) and additional hardware categories (Mini PCs, laptops).
*   **Business Model & Future Plans:** The developer plans to monetize through affiliate links and "deal alerts" for highly-rated (A/B) systems. There is also potential to build a community-driven feed of verified deals.
*   **Community Feedback:**
    *   **Positive:** Users appreciate the lightweight interface and the ability to quickly identify if a pre-built system is overpriced.
    *   **Critical:** Some users questioned the long-term viability against AI chatbots (like ChatGPT), which can perform similar comparisons. Others criticized the site's aesthetic and pointed out the omission of critical components like power supplies in the valuation engine.
    *   **Technical Suggestions:** Users suggested integrating used-market data (eBay, FB Marketplace) and expanding the pricing models to include B&H as a retailer and integrated graphics.

Overall, the community is supportive of the project's utility in the current market, where hardware prices are volatile due to high demand for AI-capable machines. The developer is actively using user feedback to iterate on the tool's features and expand its regional availability.
